\section{Introduction}

Large language models deployed as interactive agents must repeatedly decide \emph{how} to compute: reason internally, or delegate to an external tool.
A Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct agent navigating ScienceWorld \cite{scienceworld-2022}, a text-based science simulation with 30 task types, faces this choice at every step. Tracking temperature thresholds, container states, and multi-step procedures via internal reasoning is error-prone: the model may hallucinate that water has boiled when the stove was never activated, or that an object has been moved when the action was invalid. Deterministic external computation (environment simulators, code interpreters) eliminates such hallucinations via exact state transitions. The practical question for agent design is therefore: \emph{when should an agent route computation externally versus reasoning internally?}

Existing routing approaches frame this as a capability or efficiency decision.
Toolformer \cite{toolformer-2023} teaches models to insert API calls when doing so reduces perplexity; ART \cite{art-2023} decomposes tasks into tool-augmented programs; Chameleon \cite{chameleon-2023} selects among heterogeneous modules (search, code, vision) per subtask.
More recent adaptive-computation methods route to different reasoning depths \cite{cogrouter-2026,ares-2026} or model tiers \cite{mtrouter-2026}.
Concurrent analyses of when and whether to invoke tools~\citep{when2tool-2026,tool-use-tax-2026,to-call-or-not-2026} further presuppose diverse routing signals.
The shared assumption is that routing signal stems from diverse sources (accuracy, latency, capability matching) and that a learned router can exploit this signal to improve over any fixed strategy.
But no prior work has systematically decomposed what drives routing decisions in interactive environments. Without such a decomposition, the field cannot distinguish settings where diverse routing signals justify learned routers from those where a single failure mode dominates and a fixed strategy suffices.

We propose a \emph{formal diagnostic framework} for answering this question. The framework comprises (i)~episode-level counterfactual labeling under pure strategies (\S\ref{sec:collection}--\ref{sec:labeling}), and (ii)~the Death Avoidance Factor (DAF), a penalty-dependent metric that decomposes the routing score gap into death-avoidance and non-death components (\S\ref{sec:daf}). Applied to ScienceWorld, \textbf{78.9\% of non-tie routing labels arise from death asymmetry} (75 of 95), a penalty-independent finding that holds regardless of how death is penalized. Under ScienceWorld's specific penalty structure ($P{=}100$), the penalty-weighted DAF reaches $90.4\%$ (95\% CI: $[81.6\%, 98.8\%]$), consistent with the predicted value from observed $\delta{=}0.265$ and $P{=}100$.
The internal strategy's hallucination-induced failures trigger catastrophic agent death (a $-100$ penalty), while the deterministic strategy survives the same episodes.
Once death episodes are removed, the performance gap collapses to $\Delta_{\text{nd}} = +2.84$. A per-task consistency check ($r = 0.97$) confirms that the near-perfect correlation is a mathematical consequence of death dominance when $P$ is constant (\S\ref{sec:death-decomp}).

This framework addresses a methodological gap.
The standard approach to generating routing labels, per-step oracle comparison, degenerates under sparse rewards.
In ScienceWorld, non-zero reward arrives only at episode termination; 97.4\% of steps (across 11 prescreened task types) produce identical scores regardless of modality, so no step-level signal exists (\S\ref{sec:collection}).
Keyword-based heuristics also fail structurally, as ScienceWorld actions lack science-specific terminology (\S\ref{sec:baselines}).
Our counterfactual approach runs complete episodes under pure-internal (ReAct \cite{react-2023}) and pure-deterministic strategies, then compares episode outcomes to generate routing labels (\S\ref{sec:collection}). The framework is applicable to any environment with controllable modality comparison and binary catastrophic outcomes, requiring only paired episode outcomes under two modalities.

Two cross-context checks probe the specificity of this finding.
First, a MATH Level~4--5 evaluation ($N{=}795$ problems, code interpreter as deterministic modality) confirms no routing signal without catastrophic failure: internal reasoning and code interpretation achieve near-identical accuracy ($73.5\%$ vs.\ $73.0\%$, $p = 0.81$).
Second, a preliminary cross-model pilot with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (7 task types, $N{=}70$) shows direction-consistent death patterns, with a larger death-rate differential ($+34.3\%$ vs.\ $+26.6\%$ for Qwen; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model}).
Agent improvement baselines confirm that death dominance is robust: retry yields only marginal reduction, while $10{\times}$ model scaling (72B) and Reflexion~\citep{reflexion-2023} each reduce death rates to ${\sim}$35\% through independent mechanisms, yet neither closes the ${\sim}$18~pp gap to deterministic (\S\ref{sec:agent-improvement}).
An exploratory router (Qwen3 LoRA, 0.6B--4B) yields flat step-level balanced accuracy ($56$--$59\%$); at episode level, only 4B exceeds the always-deterministic baseline (\S\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}).

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{An episode-level counterfactual diagnostic framework} for decomposing routing signal in interactive environments, with dual penalty-independent and penalty-dependent metrics (Algorithm~\ref{alg:labeling}) and router training as a diagnostic probe of label informativeness. The framework requires only paired episode outcomes under two modalities with binary catastrophic indicators (\S\ref{sec:collection}--\ref{sec:daf}, \S\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}).

    \item \textbf{Evidence that death dominance is robust under three independent interventions}: 78.9\% of non-tie routing labels arise from death asymmetry, with DAF $= 90.4\%$ at $P{=}100$. Retry, $10{\times}$ model scaling, and Reflexion each fail to close the ${\sim}$18~pp gap to deterministic execution (\S\ref{sec:death-decomp}--\ref{sec:agent-improvement}).

    \item \textbf{Cross-environment boundary probes}: MATH ($N{=}795$) confirms the predicted null ($p = 0.81$); ALFWorld ($N{=}135$) identifies information asymmetry as an alternative mechanism; a Llama pilot ($N{=}70$) shows cross-model directional consistency. These are boundary probes of framework applicability, not direct replications (\S\ref{sec:math-contrast}--\ref{sec:cross-model}).
\end{enumerate}

lines: Three qualitatively different interventions all fail to close the gap to deterministic-level safety (16.3\%). Retry yields only marginal reduction (40.9\% vs.\ baseline 42.9\%, ${\sim}$2~pp across three trials; Fisher exact $p > 0.6$). $10{\times}$ capability scaling reduces death rate to ${\sim}$35\% ($\Delta \approx -17$~pp). Self-correction via Reflexion achieves a comparable reduction on death-prone tasks (${\sim}$35\%, $\Delta \approx -17$~pp). That two independent mechanisms (parameter scaling and verbal self-correction) converge to nearly identical death-rate floors suggests a shared bound set by the internal strategy's lack of ground-truth state access, not by any single intervention's limitations. Death dominance is robust under all three tested interventions. \texttt{find-non-living-thing} exhibits 0\% death across all conditions, confirming that death risk is task-specific. Compounding state estimation errors across multi-step trajectories create catastrophic failures that single-axis improvements attenuate but do not eliminate. Tree search with environment feedback and frontier models remain untested. Prior tool-routing work \citep{toolformer-2023,art-2023,chameleon-2023} operates in non-interactive settings where individual tool calls are independent; in multi-step interactive environments, the finding is not that death exists but that the death-rate differential ($\delta = 26.6$~pp) and its downstream effects resist all three tested intervention axes.

+The oracle router matches always-deterministic on 96.3\% of decisions, improving score by only 2.89 points ($-6.58$ vs.\ $-9.47$). This \emph{oracle degeneracy} challenges a core assumption of routing research: that learning to switch between modalities yields substantial gains over any fixed strategy. When death dominance holds, the optimal policy is near-degenerate because the dominant signal (avoiding catastrophic failure) uniformly favors deterministic computation. Practitioners should first verify that the oracle margin justifies the complexity of a learned router before investing in routing infrastructure.

Stronger backbones lower death rates but do not eliminate death dominance: Qwen2.5-72B reduces aggregate death from ${\sim}$51\% to ${\sim}$35\% ($-17$~pp), yet DAF remains $90.9\%$ (vs.\ $90.4\%$ at 7B), and the gap to deterministic (16.3\%) remains ${\sim}$18~pp. The Llama pilot ($\delta = +34.3\%$) versus Qwen-7B ($\delta = +26.6\%$) is consistent in the capability-increase direction. Preliminary evidence (Qwen2.5-0.5B, $N{=}15$) suggests the relationship is non-monotonic: very weak models exhibit low death rates from inability to reach dangerous states. Our results suggest that in environments where one modality triggers irreversible catastrophic failures with severe penalties, death avoidance will dominate routing signal; self-correction mechanisms can selectively reduce death-driven signal but are unlikely to eliminate death dominance.

+Our framework provides a practical diagnostic sequence for practitioners deploying modular agents. First, identify whether the target environment contains catastrophic failure mechanisms (permadeath, irreversible penalties). Second, estimate the death-rate asymmetry between internal and deterministic strategies using a small pilot (${\sim}$50 episodes suffice for directional signal). Third, if the resulting DAF exceeds ${\sim}$50\% or the death-asymmetry label fraction exceeds ${\sim}$60\%, a fixed deterministic strategy is likely to match or exceed a learned router at substantially lower deployment complexity. The MATH negative control ($p = 0.81$) confirms that this diagnostic correctly identifies environments where routing adds no value.

DAF increases monotonically with $P$ (Appendix~\ref{app:penalty}); the penalty-independent label fraction (78.9\%) is the more informative primary diagnostic. The framework requires paired episodes under two modalities, binary catastrophic outcomes, and sparse rewards. ScienceWorld satisfies all three; MATH lacks catastrophic outcomes (negative control); ALFWorld lacks them too, and the framework identifies information asymmetry as the alternative mechanism. When $P$ is small relative to $\Delta_{\text{nd}}$, DAF degrades (at $P{=}0$, DAF $= 7.5\%$); the framework is most informative when catastrophic penalties dominate non-death score differences. NetHack~\citep{nethack-2020} and Crafter~\citep{crafter-2022}, both featuring permadeath, are the most direct replication targets.

\section{Introduction}

Large language models deployed as interactive agents must repeatedly decide \emph{how} to compute: reason internally, or delegate to an external tool.
A Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct agent navigating ScienceWorld \cite{scienceworld-2022}, a text-based science simulation with 30 task types, faces this choice at every step. Tracking temperature thresholds, container states, and multi-step procedures via internal reasoning is error-prone: the model may hallucinate that water has boiled when the stove was never activated, or that an object has been moved when the action was invalid. Deterministic external computation (environment simulators, code interpreters) eliminates such hallucinations via exact state transitions. The practical question for agent design is therefore: \emph{when should an agent route computation externally versus reasoning internally?}

Existing routing approaches frame this as a capability or efficiency decision.
Toolformer \cite{toolformer-2023} teaches models to insert API calls when doing so reduces perplexity; ART \cite{art-2023} decomposes tasks into tool-augmented programs; Chameleon \cite{chameleon-2023} selects among heterogeneous modules (search, code, vision) per subtask.
More recent adaptive-computation methods route to different reasoning depths \cite{cogrouter-2026,ares-2026} or model tiers \cite{mtrouter-2026}.
Concurrent analyses of when and whether to invoke tools~\citep{when2tool-2026,tool-use-tax-2026,to-call-or-not-2026} further presuppose diverse routing signals.
The shared assumption is that routing signal stems from diverse sources (accuracy, latency, capability matching) and that a learned router can exploit this signal to improve over any fixed strategy.
But no prior work has systematically decomposed what drives routing decisions in interactive environments. Without such a decomposition, the field cannot distinguish settings where diverse routing signals justify learned routers from those where a single failure mode dominates and a fixed strategy suffices.

We propose a \emph{formal diagnostic framework} for answering this question. The framework comprises (i)~episode-level counterfactual labeling under pure strategies (\S\ref{sec:collection}--\ref{sec:labeling}), and (ii)~the Death Avoidance Factor (DAF), a penalty-dependent metric that decomposes the routing score gap into death-avoidance and non-death components (\S\ref{sec:daf}). Applied to ScienceWorld, \textbf{78.9\% of non-tie routing labels arise from death asymmetry} (75 of 95), a penalty-independent finding that holds regardless of how death is penalized. Under ScienceWorld's specific penalty structure ($P{=}100$), the penalty-weighted DAF reaches $90.4\%$ (95\% CI: $[81.6\%, 98.8\%]$), consistent with the predicted value from observed $\delta{=}0.265$ and $P{=}100$.
The internal strategy's hallucination-induced failures trigger catastrophic agent death (a $-100$ penalty), while the deterministic strategy survives the same episodes.
Once death episodes are removed, the performance gap collapses to $\Delta_{\text{nd}} = +2.84$. A per-task consistency check ($r = 0.97$) confirms that the near-perfect correlation is a mathematical consequence of death dominance when $P$ is constant (\S\ref{sec:death-decomp}).

This framework addresses a methodological gap.
The standard approach to generating routing labels, per-step oracle comparison, degenerates under sparse rewards.
In ScienceWorld, non-zero reward arrives only at episode termination; 97.4\% of steps (across 11 prescreened task types) produce identical scores regardless of modality, so no step-level signal exists (\S\ref{sec:collection}).
Keyword-based heuristics also fail structurally, as ScienceWorld actions lack science-specific terminology (\S\ref{sec:baselines}).
Our counterfactual approach runs complete episodes under pure-internal (ReAct \cite{react-2023}) and pure-deterministic strategies, then compares episode outcomes to generate routing labels (\S\ref{sec:collection}). The framework is applicable to any environment with controllable modality comparison and binary catastrophic outcomes, requiring only paired episode outcomes under two modalities.

Two cross-context checks probe the specificity of this finding.
First, a MATH Level~4--5 evaluation ($N{=}795$ problems, code interpreter as deterministic modality) confirms no routing signal without catastrophic failure: internal reasoning and code interpretation achieve near-identical accuracy ($73.5\%$ vs.\ $73.0\%$, $p = 0.81$).
Second, a preliminary cross-model pilot with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (7 task types, $N{=}70$) shows direction-consistent death patterns, with a larger death-rate differential ($+34.3\%$ vs.\ $+26.6\%$ for Qwen; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model}).
Agent improvement baselines confirm that death dominance is robust: retry yields only marginal reduction, while $10{\times}$ model scaling (72B) and Reflexion~\citep{reflexion-2023} each reduce death rates to ${\sim}$35\% through independent mechanisms, yet neither closes the ${\sim}$18~pp gap to deterministic (\S\ref{sec:agent-improvement}).
An exploratory router (Qwen3 LoRA, 0.6B--4B) yields flat step-level balanced accuracy ($56$--$59\%$); at episode level, only 4B exceeds the always-deterministic baseline (\S\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}).

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{An episode-level counterfactual diagnostic framework} for decomposing routing signal in interactive environments, with dual penalty-independent and penalty-dependent metrics (Algorithm~\ref{alg:labeling}) and router training as a diagnostic probe of label informativeness. The framework requires only paired episode outcomes under two modalities with binary catastrophic indicators (\S\ref{sec:collection}--\ref{sec:daf}, \S\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}).

    \item \textbf{Evidence that death dominance is robust and routing value is near-degenerate}: 78.9\% of non-tie routing labels arise from death asymmetry, with DAF $= 90.4\%$ at $P{=}100$. The oracle router degenerates to unconditional deterministic computation (96.3\% decision overlap). Retry, $10{\times}$ model scaling, and Reflexion each fail to close the ${\sim}$18~pp gap to deterministic execution (\S\ref{sec:death-decomp}--\ref{sec:agent-improvement}).

    \item \textbf{Cross-environment boundary probes}: MATH ($N{=}795$) confirms the predicted null ($p = 0.81$); ALFWorld ($N{=}135$) identifies information asymmetry as an alternative mechanism; a Llama pilot ($N{=}70$) shows cross-model directional consistency. These are boundary probes of framework applicability, not direct replications (\S\ref{sec:math-contrast}--\ref{sec:cross-model}).
\end{enumerate}
